statement: A dealer auction app that keeps a reference price, the inspection report and a six-stage settlement in view at every step of a used-car deal.
team: Product designer, working alongside product and development colleagues
heroCaption: The car page with its price block, the bid sheet, and the order list numbered one to six: the dealer's path from a price to a plate release.

snapshot.problem: Dealers had to price, inspect and pay for used cars they had not seen, in a market that runs on opaque prices and personal trust.
snapshot.role: Product designer across the dealer app: market structure, bidding, negotiation and settlement states, the listing flow, memberships, and light and dark themes in Persian.
snapshot.result: Version 3.1 of the dealer app drawn as 241 phone screens in 43 sections, with a 24-screen prototype for transaction states.

context.heading: The trade side of a used-car marketplace
body: Khodro45 is an Iranian online marketplace for used cars. Sellers list cars on it; this app is the other side, where the trade buys them. Its splash screen reads Dealer App V.3.1, so the file is a version of a working product rather than a first concept.

Sign-up asks a new user to choose one of three activities: dealership owner, broker or car-sector investor. Behind the entry sits a services hub that reaches past buying and selling into owning a car: traffic fines, transfer tax, insurance, parts, servicing, inspection and daily prices.

problem.heading: Three questions a dealer could not answer
body: A dealer buying a car they have not seen needs three answers: what it is worth, what condition it is really in, and who holds the money until the title changes hands. A classified listing answers none of them.

The file answers each with a mechanism: a reference price beside every offer, an inspection report inside the car page, and a settlement that moves through six numbered stages, with a guarantee held by Khodro45 until the last one is done.

markets.heading: Three markets, one car page
body: The app has three market lists, drawn as separate sections rather than one list with a filter: Live, the live auction; Market, which the app's tabs call the showroom; and Bazaar. Each has its own version of the car page.

They differ in what sits next to the price. Live cards show the dealer's own bid, whether it is winning, losing or extended, and the fair market price. Market cards show the last offer against the seller's asking price and a label for how close the deal is. Bazaar cards show the time left, the highest bid and the fair market price.
The car page keeps the same split. Live and Bazaar set the highest bid against the fair market price; Market sets the last offer against the seller's asking price.

solution.heading: Price and condition at the point of commitment
body: The car page is one long scroll: photos, the price block, then the inspection report. The report opens on the car's facts (intake number, trim, mileage, gearbox, options, remaining insurance and a roadworthiness certificate) and scores each system out of five.

Body and tyres get a damage map that colour-codes panels replaced or fully repainted, dented, or scratched. Chassis and pillar findings are listed part by part, each with a verdict and, where a part has failed, a photo.

Bidding happens in a sheet over the car page. Beside a manual bid, a dealer can set an automatic bid with its own step. A costs sheet itemises what the price does not include, and a notice states that the body inspection is guaranteed by Khodro45.

settlement.heading: Six stages, each with a clock
body: Winning a car starts a settlement that the order list numbers from one to six: the owner's documents are verified, the dealer pays a deposit, then the final settlement, the settlement is confirmed, the car is handed over with a power of attorney, and the plate is released.
Each card names its stage and the next one, and most carry a countdown. A plate-release guarantee is held along the way; the order page states that Khodro45 pays it back once the release is recorded.

Before settlement comes negotiation. The order list shows every state a deal can be in: ready to negotiate, negotiating, renegotiating, accepted, needs a higher offer, needs a new offer, awaiting approval, completed, and cancelled for lack of agreement. A 24-screen prototype walks one order through them.

selling.heading: The dealer as a seller
body: Dealers sell as well as buy. A car is added through a stepped form (brand, model, year, trim, mileage, colour, city, VIN and plate), then questions about ownership and condition: first owner or not, whether the ownership card is in the dealer's name, a spare key, accidents, body damage, mechanical problems and tyres.

The form hands over to a self-inspection. A photo guide covers light, a clean car, distance and holding the phone sideways. The upload screens ask for each angle, a 15-second engine video with sound, documents and defects, with damaged panels marked on a map of the car.

The car then appears in the dealer's own list, where its listing and its auction can each be switched on or off. Its page shows views and messages in total and for each platform it is listed on: Khodro45, Divar, Bama and Sheypoor.

business.heading: Paying for access, or earning by volume
body: The file keeps two dealer memberships. In one, a dealer must buy one of five annual subscriptions before using the app, and each level caps the total they can bid on, from 500 million toman up to unlimited.

In the other, a Customer Club, dealers climb tiers by trading volume over twelve months and earn rewards: credit up to 500 million toman, free delivery of the power of attorney and three free car transports. The file does not say whether one replaced the other.
A dealer score sits beside both: a rating out of five, updated monthly from settlement speed, plate-release speed, withdrawals, cancellations and the number of deals in the last 100 days.

method.heading: Tested as flows, in two themes
body: Almost every section is drawn twice, once dark and once light: 110 dark and 127 light screens across the sections. A prototype entry board, titled Welcome to Design Play Ground, lets a tester choose dark or light and then a path through the app.

Transaction status has a prototype of its own. Its 24 screens take one order through negotiation, the seller's counter-offer and the deposit, where countdowns and penalties make an unclear state expensive.

process.heading: The six settlement stages, as the order list numbers them

steps.label: Owner's documents
steps.note: Verified first; the deposit button stays disabled until they are.

steps.label: Deposit
steps.note: Paid within a countdown shown on the card.

steps.label: Final settlement
steps.note: The rest of the price, on its own clock.

steps.label: Confirmation
steps.note: The settlement is confirmed before the car moves.

steps.label: Handover
steps.note: The car and a power of attorney change hands; the contract balance is paid.

steps.label: Plate release
steps.note: A receipt is uploaded, and the guarantee is paid back.

decisions.heading: Decisions the file makes visible
decisions.lede: Read from the screens and their states, not from a written rationale; the file has none.

items.title: Always show a reference price
items.why: No offer in the app stands alone. Live and Bazaar set it against a fair market price, Market against the seller's asking price, and the bid sheet repeats the reference where the dealer types a number.
items.tradeoff: The reference changes with the market, so a dealer has to know which number they are being measured against.
items.evidence: The Live and Market price blocks, and the bid sheet.

items.title: Put the inspection inside the car page
items.why: The report is a set of tabs on the car page (car facts, body and tyres, engine, electrical), not a separate document. A damage map colours the affected panels, and every failed part carries a photo.
items.evidence: The car facts and the body and chassis findings of the report.

items.title: Name every state and give it a clock
items.why: An order is always in a named state with its next step written on the card, and most states carry a countdown. The 3:14 warning says when an offer will be withdrawn automatically and a penalty applied.
items.evidence: The order list with its states, and the six numbered stages.

items.title: Warn before reopening the auction
items.why: In negotiation, rejecting the seller's price and entering your own reopens the auction to other bidders. The sheet says so in full and, in one version, asks the dealer to tick a box before submitting.
items.tradeoff: One more step at the moment a dealer is trying to close.
items.evidence: The two negotiation sheets from the prototype.

items.title: Show every cost before the commitment
items.why: The service fee sits in the price block, and a costs sheet lists the rest (municipal charges, transport, title transfer and plate release) with a total, reachable from the car page before any bid.
items.evidence: The costs sheet beside the bid.

items.title: A price needs a neighbour
items.body: A bid means little on its own. Every price in the app sits beside another one (fair price, seller's ask or last offer), so the dealer judges a gap rather than a figure.

items.title: In a transaction, the states are the product
items.body: Most screens after a win are the same card in a different state. Naming each state, its next step and its deadline was the design work; the layout barely changes.

items.title: Access fees work against a marketplace
items.body: An auction needs participation. A subscription that caps bidding limits exactly that, and a club that rewards volume pushes the other way. Keeping both in the file makes the trade-off visible.
